function.name: get_cell_function
function.description: Get the information about cell functions based on its part. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

cell_part.description: The part of the cell, e.g. mitochondria

detail_level.description: The level of detail for the cell function information.

**How to Identify (and Count) Mitochondria in a Cell** Below is a practical workflow that combines several complementary techniques. Choose the approach that best fits your resources, the cell type you’re studying, and the level of precision you need. | Step | What to Do | Why It Matters | Tips & Common Pitfalls | |------|------------|----------------|------------------------| | **1. Define the Goal** | Decide whether you need an *absolute count*, a *relative estimate*, or a *dynamic measurement* (e.g., changes over time). | Different goals require different methods (e.g., fixed‑cell imaging vs. live‑cell tracking). | Clarify the biological question early (e.g., “How many mitochondria per hepatocyte?”). | | **2. Choose a Labeling Strategy** | • **Fluorescent dyes** (MitoTracker, JC‑1, TMRE)
• **Immunofluorescence** (anti‑COX IV, anti‑VDAC)
• **Genetically encoded tags** (mito‑GFP, mito‑mCherry)
• **Electron microscopy** (fixed cells, thin sections) | Each method has trade‑offs in specificity, phototoxicity, and resolution. | For live imaging, use low‑toxic dyes; for fixed cells, fix with paraformaldehyde + glutaraldehyde for EM. | | **3. Prepare Samples** | • **Live‑cell imaging**: Plate cells on glass‑bottom dishes, keep at 37 °C, 5 % CO₂.
• **Fixed imaging**: Fix with 4 % PFA (10 min), permeabilize with 0.1 % Triton X‑100 (5 min).
• **EM**: Fix with 2.5 % glutaraldehyde, post‑fix with 1 % osmium tetroxide, dehydrate, embed in epoxy resin. | Proper fixation preserves ultrastructure and antigenicity. | Avoid over‑fixation; it can mask epitopes and shrink mitochondria. | | **4. Acquire Images** | • **Confocal / Spinning‑disk**: Z‑stacks to capture entire cell volume.
• **Super‑resolution (STED, SIM)**: For sub‑mitochondrial detail.
• **EM**: Serial sections for 3‑D reconstruction. | High‑resolution images are essential for accurate counting. | Use identical laser power and detector settings across samples for comparability. | | **5. Image Processing & Segmentation** | • **Background subtraction** (rolling ball).
• **Thresholding** (Otsu, adaptive).
• **Watershed** or **machine‑learning** (Cellpose, Ilastik) to separate touching mitochondria. | Accurate segmentation directly affects count accuracy. | Validate segmentation manually on a subset of images. | | **6. Counting** | • **Manual counting** (ImageJ ROI Manager).
• **Automated counting** (CellProfiler pipeline).
• **3‑D reconstruction** (Imaris, Amira) for EM data. | Automation speeds up throughput but requires validation. | For live imaging, track mitochondria over time to assess dynamics. | | **7. Normalization & Reporting** | • Normalize counts to cell area, volume, or protein content.
• Report mean ± SD, n (number of cells), and statistical tests. | Normalization allows comparison across experiments and cell types. | Include raw counts, normalized values, and confidence intervals. | | **8. Optional – Quantify mtDNA Copy Number** | • Extract total DNA, perform qPCR for mtDNA (e.g., ND1) vs nuclear gene (β‑actin). | mtDNA copy number correlates with mitochondrial abundance but is indirect. | Use validated primers and standard curves. | --- ### Quick‑Start Protocol (Fluorescent Dye + Confocal) 1. **Cell Seeding** - Seed 1 × 10⁵ cells per 35 mm dish with glass bottom. - Incubate overnight at 37 °C, 5 % CO₂. 2. **Staining** - Prepare MitoTracker Red CMXRos (200 nM) in pre‑warmed DMEM. - Replace medium with dye solution, incubate 30 min at 37 °C. - Wash twice with warm PBS. 3. **Imaging** - Mount dish on confocal microscope. - Acquire Z‑stack (step size 0.3 µm) covering entire cell. - Use 488 nm excitation, 600–650 nm emission. 4. **Processing** - Import stack into ImageJ. - Apply 3‑D deconvolution (if available). - Use “Analyze Particles” after thresholding; set size filter (e.g., 0.1–5 µm²). - Export particle count. 5. **Analysis** - Repeat for at least 30 cells per condition. - Compute mean ± SD. - Perform t‑test or ANOVA if comparing groups. --- ### Advanced Options | Technique | When to Use | Key Advantages | Key Challenges | |-----------|-------------|----------------|----------------| | **Live‑cell tracking** (e.g., using CellProfiler’s “Track Objects”) | Studying mitochondrial fission/fusion dynamics | Real‑time insight into turnover | Requires high‑speed imaging, photobleaching control | | **Super‑resolution** (SIM/STED) | Resolving cristae or small organelles | ~50 nm resolution | Longer acquisition, higher phototoxicity | | **Electron tomography** | Precise 3‑D ultrastructure | Near‑atomic detail | Labor‑intensive, requires specialized equipment | | **Flow cytometry** (MitoTracker + FSC/SSC) | Rapid bulk measurement | High throughput | Cannot resolve individual mitochondria within a cell | --- ### Practical Tips 1. **Controls** - Include unstained cells to assess autofluorescence. - Use a mitochondrial uncoupler (FCCP) to confirm dye specificity. 2. **Photobleaching** - Minimize laser exposure; use neutral density filters if needed. 3. **Data Management** - Store raw images with metadata (date, instrument, settings). - Use versioned analysis scripts (Python, R, MATLAB). 4. **Reproducibility** - Document every step in a lab notebook or electronic lab notebook (ELN). - Share analysis pipelines via GitHub or similar platforms. --- ### Quick Reference: Mitochondrial Count per Cell Type (Typical Ranges) | Cell Type | Typical Mitochondria per Cell | Notes | |-----------|------------------------------|-------| | HeLa | 200–400 | Highly proliferative | | Hepatocyte | 500–800 | Energy‑rich | | Neuron (axon) | 10⁴–10⁵ | Dense network | | Cardiomyocyte | 10⁵–10⁶ | High ATP demand | | Fibroblast | 100–300 | Variable with passage | *(Values are approximate and depend on culture conditions.)* --- ### Final Thought Counting mitochondria is not just a technical exercise—it informs on cellular bioenergetics, disease states, and developmental biology. By combining robust labeling, high‑resolution imaging, and rigorous image analysis, you can obtain reliable, reproducible counts that will strengthen your scientific conclusions. Happy imaging!
